newsitem.title: USA: Negotiators hope to announce tobacco deal Friday.
newsitem.headline: Negotiators hope to announce tobacco deal Friday.

text.p: State attorneys general and negotiators for the tobacco industry hoped to announce on Friday a landmark agreement that would require the companies to pay as much as $370 billion to settle lawsuits and fund anti-smoking efforts.

In a sweeping agreement with U.S. states and lawyers for smokers, the tobacco companies would settle hundreds of lawsuits, launch major new anti-smoking programs, sharply curtail cigarette advertising and submit to tough new government regulation.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a key negotiator for U.S. states suing the tobacco industry, told reporters as meetings began on Friday morning: "I hope we'll have some good news for you today."
Negotiators met late Thursday and early Friday morning trying to iron out remaining issues.

Sources close to the talks said the industry had made major concessions in the area of Food and Drug Administration regulation that would give the government agency the power to regulate cigarettes as a drug delivery device.

But negotiators were still trying to finalize details of what statement each tobacco company would make about the health risks of smoking, and what industry documents would be disclosed. The negotiators were also discussing provisions to protect so-called whistle blowers, or employees of cigarette companies who provide evidence against their employers.

Sources close to the talks said the parties plan to propose a total settlement package of about $370 billion. Part of the package, about $50 billion, would be to "punish" the industry. That amount would be used to pay for health coverage for uninsured children, sources said.

As part of the deal, individuals suing the tobacco industry would not be able to seek punitive damages for past behavior by the industry. However, they would be able to seek such damages for future wrongdoing.

Talks between tobacco industry representatives and the state attorneys general have been going on since early April. The negotiations are aimed at a broad settlement of the huge legal claims against the industry in return for increased regulation, advertising curbs and health care programs.

Forty states have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of treating sick smokers. The states are demanding that the industry agree to be punished for past actions, that it pay damages for smoking-related injuries and that it agree to allow the Food and Drug Administration to regulate cigarettes as a drug.

The states want to wind up the talks this week. If there is no agreement, Moore has said he will go ahead with presenting Mississippi's case against the industry at the first trial of a state suit, set for July 7.

Any agreement would have to be approved by President Bill Clinton and by Congress. Negotiators have been keeping in close touch with a key Clinton aide, Bruce Lindsey, who stayed in Washington to monitor the tobacco talks rather than go with Clinton to Denver for a summit of world leaders.
The stocks of tobacco companies, which gained Thursday in anticipation of an agreement, were slightly higher in early trading Friday.
The companies have declined comment on the talks.
